editorials.title: Triple test, adrift: On the ruling on definition of ‘industry’
editorials.passage:
On August 20, a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India delivered a judgment on the correctness of the ruling in Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board vs A. Rajappa (BWSSB) (1978). In that judgment, Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer had laid down what was called the “Triple Test” on what counts as an “industry” under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes (ID) Act, 1947 (ID Act). Three conditions were to be met for an industry — a systematic activity, employer-employee cooperation, and production/distribution of goods and services to satisfy human wants other than those that are purely religious or spiritual. Profit motive was irrelevant; what mattered in this determination was the nature of the activity, and only “sovereign functions” stood outside it. A five-judge Bench in State of U.P. vs Jai Bir Singh (2005) raised a doubt about this definition and a seven-judge Bench sent it to the current nine-judge Bench. This Bench, led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, left the Triple Test standing for all pending disputes under the older ID Act, which was repealed on November 21, 2025 when the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (IRC) came into force. However, a majority of the nine-judge Bench also ruled that BWSSB will not be a “sheet anchor” for interpreting Section 2(p) of the IRC. That is a mistake. In her dissenting opinion, Justice B.V. Nagarathna held that the reference itself was unnecessary and that the Triple Test requires no interference — a view shared by three other judges. Her reasoning is compelling. Since 1978, and particularly after the liberalisation and privatisation reforms of 1991, a far higher number of workers have moved to the private sector, out of the security of public employment. An expansive definition of industry, as entailed in the Triple Test, is therefore even more necessary now as a bulwark for the worker.

Yet, Section 2(p) of the IRC does not move away from Justice Krishna Iyer’s Triple Test formula in BWSSB and reproduces much of its essence. It is therefore difficult to understand why BWSSB has to be set aside when Section 2(p) itself comes up for interpretation. The Triple Test was also not merely a pro-labour device. An expansive definition of industry brought with it not just the ID Act’s protections but also its restrictions — for instance, a regulated route to retrenchment and closure for the employer, and a bar on workers striking at will. In essence, the Triple Test allowed for industrial peace rather than worker welfare alone. Severing that principle from the IRC, as the majority has done, cuts away the interpretive framework that allowed such disputes to be resolved. With the essence of the Triple Test carried into Section 2(p), it is now incumbent upon courts and tribunals to ensure that a change of statute is not read as a change of intent even if the majority judgment has removed the anchor to do so.

editorial_metadata.title: Triple test, adrift: On the ruling on definition of ‘industry’
editorial_metadata.subtitle: The Supreme Court's decision on industrial disputes risks undermining crucial labour protections and legislative intent.
editorial_metadata.author: Editorial Board

analysis.analysis_summary: The author adopts a critical tone regarding the Supreme Court's majority ruling that disconnects the established 'Triple Test' from the new Industrial Relations Code. This perspective is taken because discarding this landmark precedent weakens key safeguards for private sector workers while disrupting a balanced mechanism for resolving workplace disputes. Ultimately, the editorial contends that judicial bodies must continue preserving the original legislative intent of industrial stability despite the court's verdict.

editorials.title: Core concerns: On the Indian economy, the road ahead
editorials.passage:
The slowdown in the growth of India’s core industrial sectors in July was not surprising, with other indicators predicting easing demand conditions as well. Growth in the index of core industries (ICI) slowed to 5.4% in July from 6% in the previous month. This was in keeping with the Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index, which in July eased to its lowest level since August 2021 due to weak domestic demand conditions. While July’s growth in the ICI was the second-highest growth rate in the last seven months, the data nevertheless highlight some concerning aspects of the Indian economy. The first has to do with the fact that a large part of even this slower growth seems to be based on a statistical low base effect. The coal sector, for example, grew at an 11-month high of 7.6% in July, but this was based on a contraction of 12.3% in July of last year. Similarly, the refinery products sector snapped a three-month streak of contraction to grow at 2.7%, but this too was based on a contraction in July 2025. The iron ore sector, however, grew at a very robust 29.5%, albeit slower than a blistering 44.5% in June. This seems heartening regardless of the contractions of 16.4% and 7.1% in June and July of last year, respectively. But the steel sector slowed drastically in July to 2.9% from 5.6% in June and 15.7% in July of last year.

The domestic crude oil and natural gas sectors have been lasting drags on the economy. Both have contracted continuously for at least the last 14 months for which the new series of the ICI has data. India’s crude oil imports rose 13.3% in volume terms in July, while Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) imports grew a more marginal 1.5%, showing that the economy’s appetite is being whetted from abroad. This external dependence is proving very expensive. High oil prices have meant that the crude oil import bill jumped 41% in July. The 100% tariffs that the United States is preparing to levy on countries such as India that import Russian oil will once again burden Indian exporters. Moving to 20% ethanol-blending has not yet impacted oil imports materially. Within the ICI, the only two bright spots of the economy were the cement and electricity sectors. The electricity sector grew at a robust 9% in July, although this was slower than the two consecutive months of double-digit growth in May and June thanks to the prevalent heatwave conditions in many parts of the country. The cement sector sped up to 13.1%, a welcome acceleration. Such positive trends were few and far between. Overall, the Indian economy looks to be in for a period of slack demand, higher costs, and moderating growth.

editorial_metadata.title: Core concerns: On the Indian economy, the road ahead
editorial_metadata.subtitle: Sluggish industrial core growth signals upcoming economic headwinds and softening domestic consumer demand.
editorial_metadata.author: Editorial Board

analysis.analysis_summary: The author adopts a cautious tone to evaluate India's recent economic performance, highlighting that headline core growth is largely inflated by a statistical base effect rather than genuine expansion. Persistent drag in domestic crude oil output combined with external tariff risks indicates a challenging road ahead. By balancing weak domestic indicators against a few temporary bright spots like cement, the editorial stresses the need to prepare for sluggish demand and higher import costs.

editorials.title: To build Delhi’s future, learn from past missteps
editorials.passage:
About 25 years ago, when Delhi’s third Master Plan came into effect, the city’s population was about 14 million, Gurugram and Noida were fledgling suburbs, the first lines of the capital’s Metro network were being laid, and a CNG policy for public transport had been introduced as a pollution-control measure. Since then, another 10 million people have made the capital their home, civic infrastructure of its neighbouring cities has come under acute stress, and the improvement in air quality that Delhi experienced for much of the 2000s and early 2010s has given way to an almost intractable pollution crisis. Delhi’s fourth Master Plan, notified last week, acknowledges these challenges. Its emphasis on expanding public transport, ecological restoration, redevelopment, affordable housing and mixed land use is welcome.

One of the plan’s strengths is its recognition that Delhi cannot be built simply by expanding outward. With limited land available within the National Capital Territory, better utilisation of existing urban land will become more important. The proposed increase in housing supply, including an ambition of roughly 40 lakh additional homes by 2047 at affordable rates, and greater flexibility in development norms to permit higher densities is, therefore, significant. The plan also recognises the futility of rigidly demarcating residential and commercial areas. If implemented well, these measures could ease the city’s longstanding traffic congestion and improve air quality. Mixed land use, environment-friendly transport, the redevelopment and nurturing of green spaces, and greater attention to the city’s water bodies could all contribute to improving Delhi’s ecological health and enhance the well-being of its residents.

None of these ideas will succeed, however, without confronting the national capital’s most persistent governance problems: Municipal inertia and a lack of alignment among civic agencies, Centre and Delhi government. These deficits were the biggest bottleneck in realising the previous Master Plan’s vision of a more sustainable city. Over the past 25 years, research on pollution, Yamuna restoration, waste management, urban flooding and transport development has pointed to the need for concerted action among departments. Metro expansion, for instance, works best when bus routes, last-mile connectivity, parking rules and pedestrian facilities are designed around it. Land-use planning and infrastructure development cannot be divorced from the requirements of curbing water logging, while building approvals, fire safety and emergency response require effective information-sharing among construction, fire and municipal authorities. Repeated fire incidents, building collapses and the strain placed on the city’s infrastructure during heavy rainfall have exposed the risks of fragmented and overlapping responsibilities among its agencies. Delhi has a blueprint for improving liveability. It needs to learn from past failures.

editorial_metadata.title: To build Delhi’s future, learn from past missteps
editorial_metadata.subtitle: Delhi’s latest Master Plan must overcome bureaucratic inertia and agency fragmentation to succeed.
editorial_metadata.author: Editorial Board

analysis.analysis_summary: The author adopts a pragmatic tone to evaluate Delhi's new Master Plan, welcoming its forward-looking urban and ecological vision while highlighting chronic institutional bottlenecks. The editorial contends that comprehensive urban plans inevitably fail without synchronized governance between municipal, state, and central bodies. It concludes by stressing that the capital must actively learn from past implementation deficits to build a sustainable, liveable future.
